newsitem.title: FRANCE: Clinton-style Chirac seeks bond with French youth.
newsitem.headline: Clinton-style Chirac seeks bond with French youth.

text.p: Jacques Chirac has been watching Bill Clinton and it shows.

The French president drew several lessons from the U.S. leader's political manual in an upbeat Monday night television interview designed to appeal to young people with a drive for computers and literacy in schools to prepare them for the information age.

The setting was unmistakably French: no other Western democracy allows its ruler to speak unopposed on prime-time television for two hours about the subjects of his choice with the interviewers of his choice at the time of his choice.
There was none of the cut-and-thrust of a White House news conference or the jousting of a British tv interview.
The left-of-centre newspaper Le Monde denounced the show "The year 2000: a chance for all?" as "an advertising slot".

Chirac's style was more familiar and less patrician than his predecessors'. Analysts said he talked like an "elder brother" to the young voters who helped elect him in 1995 but have since been engulfed by joblessness and gloom.
Like Clinton, he tried to reach over the heads of the political establishment and commune with ordinary people, addressing their concerns about schools and drugs.
His message too drew heavily on Clinton's January inaugural address and February State of the Union speech.
"A great nation is one that knows how to integrate all its children," Chirac declared.

He promised that all French secondary schools would be linked to computer networks by year 2000 and vowed to eradicate illiteracy in children entering high-school by the end of his seven-year term in 2002.

The president disputed the widespread view that France is far behind the United States in home computers and Internet access. A suburban Paris baker's wife knew how to use a screen and keyboard better than her New York counterpart thanks to the Minitel network developed in the 1980s, he said.

Radiating unchallenged optimism, Chirac flattered French young people as "formidable" and "fantastic", interpreting their lack of faith in the government to help them find jobs as a welcome self-reliance.

"The president is trying to stamp out gloom. His obstinate good humour has something reassuring, as if the head of state had chosen the role of the 'elder-brother-president'," the conservative pro-government Le Figaro said in an editorial.

But most other commentators were less convinced by Chirac's performance, which contrasted with a December tv interview in which he blamed the French people's innate conservatism and resistance to change for the country's economic stagnation.

"Nothing in this mixture of sometimes relevant, interesting comments and platitudes gave the feeling that the black figures of youth unemployment are about to change, or the gulf between companies and the generation looking for a first job is about to be bridged," radio commentator Pierre Le Marc said.
Chirac acknowledged that the 600,000 young people aged under 25 who are out of work -- 25 percent of young school-leavers -- were a dark stain on French society.
Overall unemployment is at a record 12.7 percent, but young people are finding it even harder to get a first job.
The answer, the president said, lay in better education, computer literacy, language teaching, vocational training, careers guidance and work experience in industry.
Yet his centre-right government has just reduced the number of teachers and introduced foreign languages into primary schools without training teachers to teach them.
The only practical measure Chirac announced was a plan to cut value added tax on multimedia products and services to 5.6 percent from 20.6 percent.

His aim appeared to be largely psychological at a time when economic indicators suggest a timid revival of growth and consumer spending, and opinion polls show a modest revival in the popularity of Chirac and Prime Minister Alain Juppe.

A year before a general election, the latest poll by the CSA institute -- taken before the president's broadcast -- showed 42 percent of voters approved of Chirac's performance and 33 percent backed Juppe.
Veteran commentator Alain Duhamel said Chirac had made "a risky switch from a paternal to a fraternal presidency".

"This fraternal presidency carries a double risk: demystifying the (presidential) function and setting such concrete criteria for his own objectives that he absolutely must produce results," Duhamel said.
